judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 1003. It raises the age below which sex is always a crime, and sets a new close-in-age rule. Oklahoma's rape statute used to reach a victim under sixteen. The act raises that to under eighteen. A second section holds the line for people close in age. Before the act, sex with someone over fourteen who consented was not charged unless the older person was over eighteen. Now sex with someone sixteen or older who consented is not charged unless the older person is more than four years older. Put together, sex with anyone under sixteen is a crime whatever the ages. For a sixteen or seventeen year old it is a crime if the other person is more than four years older. The act also widens a separate rule on school staff, which now covers any student under twenty rather than students aged sixteen to nineteen. The Oklahoma House passed it 60-21. It became law without the Governor's signature.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 1393. It gives parents a signed say before a child in special education is moved to a different set of tests. Some students with a disability are tested against alternate standards rather than the standards their year group is taught to. The act makes the State Board of Education write a separate consent form for that choice. The form goes to the parent in the parent's own language. It has to explain the benefits, the risks and what the choice means in law. It has to say plainly that refusing means the child sits the regular district and state tests with help, and is taught to the general standards. It carries a consent box and a refusal box, each with a signature line. A district may not go ahead without consent unless it records real efforts to reach the parent and the parent does not answer, or unless it wins a due process hearing. If the district wants to change the child's plan on this point, it must hold a meeting with the parent and give five school days' notice. The Oklahoma House passed it 71-23. The Governor signed it.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 1601. It lets school staff add their own sick days to paid maternity leave. Six weeks of paid maternity leave for school staff already existed in Oklahoma law, and the act does not change that. What it adds is the right to make the leave longer. A worker may use sick leave they have already earned to extend it, for recovery from the birth, for bonding with the baby, or to care for the baby. No extra approval from the school board or employer is needed. The extension is capped at six more weeks. A doctor may certify that more is needed on medical grounds, up to a combined twelve weeks under federal family leave law. The worker gives notice under that federal law, and the two run at the same time. The act is called the ARCHER Act. The Oklahoma House passed it 58-27. The Governor signed it.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 3127. It narrows the job protection that medical marijuana patients have. Oklahoma law stops an employer refusing to hire, disciplining or sacking someone just for holding a medical marijuana license, or just for a positive test. That rule had exceptions, and the act widens one of them. Before, an employer could act on a positive test where the job involved safety-sensitive duties. Now an employer may act whenever it does so under a written drug and alcohol testing policy that meets the state testing law. The act also sets a zero-tolerance standard for anyone in a safety-sensitive job, whatever the employer's own policy says. It spells out that an employer may keep and enforce a written policy barring marijuana use at work or while doing the job. The Oklahoma House passed it 47-46. The Governor signed it.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 3151. It raises the minimum number of school days for districts that count instruction in hours. Oklahoma districts may meet the school year rule by days or by hours. One of the hours options let a district run as few as one hundred sixty-six days as long as it reached one thousand eighty-six hours. From the 2027-2028 school year that floor rises to one hundred seventy-three days. The hours figure does not change. The act also says that where a district holds parent-teacher conferences during the school day and counts them as instruction time, it must offer parents and guardians the choice of meeting in person. None of this takes effect unless the Legislature gives the State Department of Education at least one hundred seventy-five million dollars more in the 2028 budget year than it did in 2026. If that happens, the act starts on July 1, 2027. If not, it never becomes law. The Oklahoma House passed it 62-28. The Governor signed it.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to override the Governor's veto of House Bill 1576. It makes Medicaid cover fast gene testing for very ill children. Rapid whole genome sequencing reads a patient's whole genetic code to find the cause of an illness. Under the act it returns first results within seven days and final results within fifteen to twenty-one days. The Oklahoma Health Care Authority must cover it as a service paid for in its own right, subject to any federal approval needed. Three conditions all have to be met. The patient must be under twenty-one. The illness must be serious or sudden with no known cause, and not explained by poisoning, an environmental exposure, an infection responding normally to treatment, or injury. The patient must be in an intensive care unit or another high-dependency unit in hospital. The Authority may still apply medical need rules, and the act lists what those rules must rest on. The Oklahoma Senate voted 36-9 to override the veto. The House did the same, so the bill became law.
